title: Amanda!
book: NCERT First Flight: Textbook in English for Class X
subject: english_literature
author: Robin Klein
syllabus_note: CBSE 2025-26 English Language and Literature (184): First Flight poem 6. Assessed through poetry extracts (5 marks) and short answers (3 marks). Only short lines are quoted here; read the full poem in the NCERT textbook.

blocks.title: 'Don't do this, Amanda! Do that, Amanda!'
blocks.body: Imagine being told every minute how to sit, what to eat and when to do your homework. **Amanda** hears it all, but her mind has escaped: she is a **mermaid**, an **orphan**, and **Rapunzel** in a tower.

blocks.title: The poet
blocks.body: **Robin Klein** was an Australian writer of children's books, known for understanding young people's feelings. Amanda! shows the gap between what adults demand and what a child longs for.
blocks.future: Teachers, counsellors and parents learn from such poems how nagging can push children away.

blocks.question: Why does Amanda escape into daydreams?
options: She feels suffocated by constant nagging and wants freedom
She is bored by the sea
blocks.explanation: Her dreams are all about freedom and peace.

blocks.title: How the poem is built
blocks.body:
The poem has **two voices** that never meet:

| Stanzas | Speaker | What is said |
|---|---|---|
| **1, 3, 5, 7** | an adult, probably her mother | constant instructions: don't bite your nails, don't hunch your shoulders, sit up straight, finish your homework, tidy your room, clean your shoes, don't eat chocolate (remember your acne), look at me when I'm speaking, stop sulking |
| **2, 4, 6** (in brackets) | Amanda, in her mind | daydreams: a **mermaid** drifting in a languid emerald sea; an **orphan** roaming the streets, patterning soft dust with bare feet; **Rapunzel** in a tower, never letting down her hair |

**Amanda's dreams:**
- As a **mermaid**, she would drift blissfully in a languid **emerald sea**, the sole inhabitant: alone and free.
- As an **orphan**, she would roam the streets, patterning soft dust with her bare feet; she thinks silence is 'golden' and freedom is sweet. She is **not** really an orphan; she imagines it to be free of instructions.
- As **Rapunzel**, she would live in a tower in peace and would **never let down her bright hair**, so no one could climb up to disturb her.

**The ending:** 'Stop that sulking at once, Amanda! You're always so moody, Amanda!' and anyone would think she is nagged. The adult does not see that the nagging itself makes her moody.

blocks.question: Why are stanzas 2, 4 and 6 in brackets?
options: the poet forgot to remove them
they are Amanda's private thoughts and daydreams
blocks.explanation: They show what she imagines while she is being scolded.

blocks.question: Why does Amanda want to be Rapunzel?
options: to live alone in a tower in peace, and not let anyone up
blocks.explanation: She would never let down her bright hair.
option_feedback: For the peace of the tower.
She would not let down her hair.

blocks.title: Who is Amanda? What does she want?
blocks.body:
**Amanda's age:** about **nine to twelve**: she has homework, must tidy her room, and is warned about acne, which suggests early adolescence.

**The speaker:** probably her **mother**, who corrects every small thing.

**Is Amanda listening?** No. She seems lost in her own world; she does not answer at all.

**What she yearns for:** **freedom, peace and solitude**: no rules, no nagging.

**Is she moody?** She may seem sulky, but she is reacting to constant criticism. The poem asks adults to **listen** to children rather than only instruct them.

**Devices:** **repetition** of 'Amanda!'; **contrast** between nagging and dreaming; **allusion** to the fairy tale of **Rapunzel**; **imagery** ('languid emerald sea', 'soft dust').

blocks.question: What does Amanda yearn for?
blocks.explanation: Each daydream is about being free and alone.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Stanzas 1, 3, 5, 7: adult nagging. Stanzas 2, 4, 6 (brackets): mermaid, orphan, Rapunzel.**
- **Last line: 'You're always so moody, Amanda!'**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying Amanda is really an orphan: she only **imagines** it.
2. Saying she listens carefully: she is lost in **daydreams**.
3. Forgetting the purpose of the brackets: they hold her **thoughts**.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Two students read the poem aloud: one as the adult (stanzas 1, 3, 5, 7), one as Amanda (2, 4, 6) in a dreamy voice. Discuss how it feels to be Amanda.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Do you think instructions help children or push them away? How would you speak to Amanda?

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **From the Diary of Anne Frank:** another young girl who feels unheard.
- **The Ball Poem:** childhood feelings that adults should respect.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
What does the poem tell us about the way adults treat children? Answer in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** In Amanda!, an adult, probably her mother, gives a stream of instructions: don't bite your nails, don't hunch your shoulders, finish your homework, tidy your room, don't eat chocolate. The adult never asks how Amanda feels. Amanda does not answer; instead she escapes into daydreams, shown in brackets. She imagines being a mermaid alone in an emerald sea, an orphan free to roam the streets, and Rapunzel in a tower who will never let her hair down. All her dreams are about freedom and peace. At the end the adult calls her moody, without seeing that the nagging has made her so. The poem tells adults to guide children gently and to listen to them.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.body:
- An adult keeps instructing Amanda in stanzas 1, 3, 5 and 7.
- In brackets, Amanda dreams of being a mermaid, an orphan and Rapunzel: free and at peace.
- She is called moody, but she is reacting to constant nagging.

blocks.title: Exam tips
blocks.body:
- Explain the brackets and the two speakers.
- Name all three daydreams and what each means.
- In long answers, discuss the effect of nagging on children.

blocks.back: Amanda, in her thoughts; that is why they are in brackets.
A mermaid in an emerald sea, an orphan roaming free, and Rapunzel in a tower.
